APL Apollo Tubes shares jump 4% after 28% crash in a week as SEBI may scrutinise Tata Steel deal | Buy, sell or hold? | Stock Market News
TATASTEEL Vaamanaa Sethi Published 27 Nov 2026, 11:53 AM IST Prefer Livemint on Google APL Apollo Tubes shares rebounded over 4% in Friday's trading session. ( AI generated image ) APL Apollo Tubes shares rebounded over 4% in Friday's trading session after reports revealed that the market regulator, the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI), may scrutinise the structure of its proposed deal with Tata Steel . According to a report by Business Standard , the regulator is reportedly examining concerns related to minority shareholder interests and the applicability of related-party transaction rules. APL Apollo Tubes share price opened at ₹ 1,505 apiece today, as compared to the previous close of ₹ 1,481.50 on Thursday and touched an intraday high of ₹ 1,544.30 on 27 November. According to the report, the market regulator is examining whether all components of the proposed transaction should be evaluated collectively under the related-party transaction (RPT) framework. These include APL Apollo’s acquisition of Tata Steel’s tubes and colour-coated steel businesses, Tata Steel’s purchase of the promoters’ stake in APL Apollo, and the contract-manufacturing agreement with promoter-linked SG Spectra Under the proposed deal, APL Apollo will initially acquire Tata Steel’s tubes and colour-coated businesses for ₹ 28,000 crore, financing the purchase through borrowings. Subsequently, Tata Steel will gain majority control of the expanded APL Apollo Tubes for around ₹ 32,267 crore by buying shares from the promoters and launching an open offer for minority shareholders. Stakeholders Empowerment Services (SES) said Tata Steel should be treated as a related party with effect from November 23. It also raised concerns over whether the first tranche was deliberately kept below the 10% threshold to avoid triggering the applicable regulatory requirements. APL Apollo Tubes shares have witnessed significant selling pressure in the recent past, declining 27.82% over the past week and 30.83% in the last one month. The stock has also fallen 22.26% so far in 2026, while losing 11.73% over the past one year, indicating sustained weakness in the counter. However, the stock has delivered positive returns over the longer term. APL Apollo Tubes shares have gained 72.63% over the past five years, despite declining 9.72% over the three-year period. Brokerage firm Motilal Oswal has given ‘buy’ rating to the APL Apollo Tubes stock with a target price of 2,200, seeing an upside potential up to 33%, saying that Tata Steel will acquire a majority stake in APAT, marking a strategic partnership that is expected to strengthen its market positioning and drive long-term growth. “Over the long term, the combined APAT-Tata Steel business is expected to generate revenue/EBITDA of INR1,027b/INR100b, with EBITDA/MT expected to improve to INR7,000-8,000 from the current INR5,500-6,000 Revenue/EBITDA/PAT are expected to clock a CAGR of 17%/18%/21% over FY26-28. We reiterate our BUY rating on the stock with a TP of INR2,220,” the firm said. Meanwhile, HDFC Securities has downgraded the stock to ‘add’ from ‘buy’ with a lower target price of ₹ 1,750 per share, keeping the estimates unchanged post the recent corporate action. “We are cutting the valuation multiple to 25x, from 35x earlier. APAT announced the acquisition of the color-coated and steel tubes business of Tata Steel for INR 280bn (2.7mn MT capacity at 24.8x FY27E EBITDA). This was followed by another announcement of APAT’s promoter S Gupta Holding selling off its 26.6% stake in the company to Tata Steel at INR 2,100/share (in three tranches). Post obtaining approvals from regulatory bodies and shareholders, Tata Steel will make an open offer to acquire another 26% at INR 2,301.4/share,” the firm said in a note. articles.title: Shareholders who said no before now hold the key to APL Apollo's big bet

Shareholders who said no before now hold the key to APL Apollo's big bet | Company Business News Minority shareholders are concerned that APL Apollo will shoulder most of the borrowing used to finance Tata Steel's ₹32,266-crore takeover. ( Photo: AI generated ) Summary The vote comes amid a history of investor resistance, with five of 11 special resolutions at its 2025 and 2026 AGMs failing to secure the required 75% approval. Gift this article Check your portfolio This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you. Subscribe to enjoy similar stories. Mumbai and New Delhi: Chairman and managing director Sanjay Gupta's APL Apollo Tubes Ltd is heading into a make-or-break vote with its own shareholders. The company will need their approval for a ₹ 28,000-crore deal to buy Tata Steel Ltd's tubes and colour-coated businesses, and it will be asking an investor base that has often said no before. The transaction, which has drawn criticism from minority investors over its financing structure, comes against a backdrop of repeated resistance to management-backed proposals, with nearly half the special resolutions put to vote at the company's last two annual general meetings failing to secure the required support. The debt-funded acquisition has raised concerns among minority shareholders over whether APL Apollo will effectively shoulder much of the borrowing used to finance Tata Steel's ₹ 32,266-crore takeover. The concerns have triggered a sharp market reaction, with APL Apollo losing nearly a quarter of its market capitalization as investors continued to sell the stock since Monday. A Mint review of voting records shows that shareholders rejected five of the 11 special resolutions placed before them at APL Apollo's 2025 and 2026 annual general meetings. Such resolutions require at least 75% of votes cast to be in favour. In each instance, opposition came largely from public institutional investors, even as promoters backed the proposals, all of which were linked to employee stock option plans. While investors opposing employee stock transfer plans is not unusual and has been reported at several companies, the defeat of resolutions is less common and points to a challenge for the promoters ahead. "Minority shareholders have strongly objected to the deal and questioned its structure, setting the stage for a tougher vote—should it happen. For now, the situation remains one to watch closely," said Amit Tandon, founder and managing director of Institutional Investor Advisory Services India Ltd (IiAS). The key concern lies in the complex structure of the transaction, in which APL Apollo will buy two assets from Tata Steel for a combined ₹ 28,000 crore, funded through debt. Tata Steel, in turn, will pay ₹ 15,510 crore for the 26.38% promoter stake in the tubes manufacturing company and make an open offer for another 26% stake, costing about ₹ 16,756 crore upon full subscription. Effectively, APL Apollo will shoulder most of the debt burden for Tata Steel’s ₹ 32,266-crore takeover, investors argued. The promoter will exit at ₹ 2,100 per share, while the shareholders will be left holding a stock that traded at ₹ 1,668.15 on the BSE on Monday. Promoters, including Gupta and other family members, own 28.3% of APL Apollo. Domestic public institutions hold about 20%, while foreign institutional investors own around 34%. The remaining shares are held by non-institutional public investors. Among the largest institutional shareholders as of September-end, foreign investors included New World Fund, with a 4.85% stake, Smallcap World Fund (4.24%) and Norway's Government Pension Fund Global (2.4%). Among domestic mutual funds, ICICI Prudential Midcap Fund held 3.47%, followed by Aditya Birla Sun Life Flexi Cap Fund (2.02%), DSP Midcap Fund (1.93%) and Franklin India Midcap Fund (1.77%). The resistance to management-backed proposals is not new. At its September 2025 AGM, shareholders rejected four of the six special resolutions, all relating to APL Apollo's proposed Employees Stock Option Plan (Esop) 2025. These covered the introduction of the scheme, its extension to employees of subsidiaries and associate companies, and authorisation for an employee welfare trust to buy shares from the secondary market using company funds. APL Apollo had sought approval to issue up to 50 lakh stock options, leaving key decisions on pricing and employee eligibility to its nomination and remuneration committee. Support for the four resolutions ranged from 71.22% to 73.66%, falling short of the required threshold despite promoters voting entirely in favour. The opposition was driven by concerns over pricing, disclosures and the benefits being extended to employees of group companies. Legal & General Investment Management (LGIM), which manages $1.5 trillion in assets, opposed all four resolutions. Resistance extended beyond employee compensation. Several foreign institutional investors, including Norges Bank, the world's largest sovereign wealth fund, LGIM and British Columbia Investment Management Corporation (BCI), also opposed chairman Sanjay Gupta's reappointment. Although the resolution was passed on 21 January 2025, their objections pointed to wider concerns over the company's governance. "The roles of chairperson and CEO should not be held by the same individual. Where a company founder combines both roles, we may support this for a limited period, provided the board has put in place measures to mitigate any conflicts of interest," Norges Bank, which manages $2.2 trillion in assets, said. The opposition continued at the September 2026 AGM, when shareholders rejected a proposal to extend the company's Stock Appreciation Rights (SAR) Scheme, 2019, to employees of associate companies. The scheme allows eligible employees to benefit from an appreciation in APL Apollo's share price. The resolution received 72.26% support, with 27.74% of votes cast against it. Four other special resolutions, relating to the reappointment of independent directors, were approved. Mint had earlier reported that investors and proxy advisory firms opposed APL Apollo's proposed transaction with Tata Steel, calling its terms unfair to minority shareholders. The market backlash has prompted Tata Steel to consider restructuring the deal. Its chief executive officer, T.V. Narendran, told NDTV Profit that discussions were under way to address shareholder concerns on both sides. Investor protection is very important,” Pandey told journalists on the sidelines of Assocham’s 17th Capital Markets Conference. The regulator is yet to receive the revised contours of the proposed transaction after Tata Steel publicly indicated that it would re-examine the structure. Under takeover regulations, the draft offer document is ordinarily required to be filed within five working days of the public announcement. Sebi is expected to wait for the revised proposal before proceeding further. The regulator’s comments come after institutional investors and proxy advisory firms raised concerns over the proposed transaction, prompting Tata Steel Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer T V Narendran to assure investors that the structure would be reviewed. The proposed transaction involves Tata Steel acquiring a controlling stake in APL Apollo Tubes while APL Apollo acquires Tata Steel’s downstream tubes and colour-coated steel businesses. APL Apollo, meanwhile, would acquire Tata Steel’s downstream businesses — including its tubes division, Khopoli unit and Tata Steel Colors — for ₹28,000 crore. Tata Steel has already acquired around 9.91 per cent of APL Apollo through a block deal at ₹2,100 per share for approximately ₹5,825 crore. The proposed transaction has faced scrutiny from institutional investors and proxy advisory firms over the valuation assigned to the businesses being transferred, the financing burden on APL Apollo and safeguards for its minority shareholders. The concern centres on the simultaneous nature of the transaction: APL Apollo is expected to acquire Tata Steel’s downstream assets while Tata Steel becomes its controlling shareholder. Investors have questioned whether the structure adequately protects minority shareholders as the ownership and capital structure of APL Apollo changes. Pandey’s remarks indicate that Sebi is closely monitoring these issues, even as it awaits the revised transaction structure from the companies. The overall transaction is subject to regulatory approvals and had earlier been targeted for completion by March 2027. Inside the Tata Sons power struggle: The rules, the rift and the road ahead | Company News - Business Standard
It is the ‌second such fight in a decade for one of India's oldest and most reputed business houses, after a years-long legal battle over Tata Sons' decision to remove earlier chairman Cyrus Mistry ended in the Supreme Court upholding the decision The battle to lead India's Tata Sons, the owner of marquee brands such as Jaguar Land Rover and Tetley Tea, headed for court on Friday after the sprawling conglomerate flouted the wishes of its controlling charity arm to reappoint ​the chairman. Tata Trusts holds a stake of 66% in Tata Sons, but the latter's board re-appointed chairman ​N. Chandrasekaran and has decided to pursue a possible stock market listing, putting the power struggle at the centre of the standoff. It is the ‌second such fight in a decade for one of India's oldest and most reputed business houses, after a years-long legal battle over Tata Sons' decision to remove earlier chairman Cyrus Mistry ended in the Supreme Court upholding the decision. Here is how the current fight could play out, along with views of both sides and the complex structures, according to people familiar with the matter: Two of the seven charitable trusts that control Tata Sons asked the Mumbai high court on Thursday to declare Chandrasekaran's reappointment 'invalid, illegal, null and void', copies of internal memos reviewed by Reuters showed. They also seek court directions that key decisions by Tata Sons require complete support from the charity arm. Reuters has learnt the trusts will tell the court that the board should not have proceeded with the decision as both trust nominees did not back the chairman's reappointment. At Friday's hearing, the trusts are expected to ask for a halt to plans for a November 30 board meeting set to decide next steps towards listing if the chief of the charity arm ‌and family head Noel Tata, as trust nominee, does not vote in favour. The board of Tata Sons agrees to the stock market listing, ordered by the central bank, but the charity arm does not. Both sides have hired top lawyers to defend them and explain who can call the shots. Lawmaker and Congress party leader Abhishek Manu Singhvi is representing the Tata Trusts led by Noel Tata. Singhvi has previously said the dispute is about shareholder supremacy and the conglomerate cannot act like a "runaway board" independent of the controlling shareholder. That position is disputed by Tata Group's Chandrasekaran, who has roped in Harish Salve, a former solicitor general of India who often represented the government in global forums. In television remarks Salve has said the board's decision was in line with internal governing rules, urging the charity ​arm to get past the "I control the trusts, I control this group mindset." The Tata Trusts ‌have problems of their own that weaken their influence. Formed of several affiliated charities, they could have used their voting power to call for a shareholders' meeting to effectively oust Chandrasekaran. But a regulator has barred one of the main charities, the Sir Ratan Tata Trust, from convening its own meetings ​in a dispute over internal ‌appointments. In turn, internal rules mean the charities currently lack the power to call for a meeting of Tata Sons shareholders. The trusts can either wait for the deadlock to ‌lift, once the regulatory inquiry ends, or ask a court to lift the curbs, two people familiar with the matter said. At the heart of the dispute facing the court is the Tata Sons' governance framework known as the "articles of association", since Tata Trusts and Tata Sons ‌disagree on ​the interpretation of ​thee rules, which are not public. The charity arm says Noel Tata's opposition to the reappointment was sufficient to halt the decision. It believes such decisions cannot be made in the absence of support of a majority of the trusts' two board nominees. In this case, "majority amongst two is ‌two and not one," the charity ​arm has publicly argued. Tata Sons' lawyer Salve disagrees, saying both trust nominees voted differently, prompting a casting vote that helped reappoint the chairman under the governance rules. The latest contract involves supplying solar modules and executing the engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) work for the project. While the company has not disclosed the contract value or the customer's identity, the order adds to its project pipeline and provides visibility into business activity over the coming financial years. Waaree Renewable Technologies, a subsidiary of Waaree Energies, received a letter of award for the 120 MWp solar project after market hours on Thursday. Under the turnkey contract, the company will be responsible for supplying solar modules and undertaking the complete engineering, procurement and construction work. This means its scope of work will cover the key stages involved in executing the solar project. The contract was awarded by a domestic private limited company. However, Waaree Renewable Technologies has not identified the customer or disclosed the financial value of the order. The project is scheduled for completion during the financial year ending March 2028 (FY28), providing the company with an execution timeline extending into the next two financial years. Waaree Renewable Technologies operates in the renewable energy sector, with a focus on solar engineering, procurement and construction services. Headquartered in Mumbai, the company develops, constructs, owns and operates solar power projects and offers integrated solutions across utility-scale, commercial and industrial segments. Its business activities include rooftop and ground-mounted solar installations, floating solar projects, open-access solar farms and operations and maintenance services. Waaree Renewable Technologies shares climbed as much as 13.6% to an intraday high of ₹ 781.55 on Friday. The rally came after the stock had touched a 52-week low of ₹ 653.80 in October 2026. Despite Friday's sharp recovery, the stock remains around 35% below its 52-week high of ₹ 1,202.60, recorded in April 2026. The recent gains have improved its shorter-term performance. Waaree Renewable Technologies shares have advanced 9% over the past week and 12% over the past month. However, the broader trend remains relatively weak. The stock has declined 13% over the past three months and 23% over the past six months. On a year-to-date (YTD) basis, it has gained 22%, although it remains down 29% over the past year. The company's September-quarter performance presented a mixed picture, with revenue registering strong growth but profitability remaining under pressure. articles.text:
Denny’s welcomes Jensen Huang back as Nvidia CEO
Livestream Menu In this article Jensen Huang is back at the helm of Nvidia — and Denny's has a booth waiting for him. The American diner chain welcomed the billionaire's return as Nvidia CEO by revealing that it had reinstated a commemorative plaque marking the birthplace of the artificial intelligence chip giant after learning of its removal on Nov. 13. "Some things you just don't take off the menu. Jensen Huang is one of them," Denny's said in a post on X . The plaque marks the booth at a Denny's restaurant in Silicon Valley, California, where Huang and his co-founders discussed the idea for Nvidia, which was founded in 1993. The restaurant chain said it learned on Nov. 13, a day after Huang's resignation , that the plaque had been removed. "We put the plaque right back up where it belongs," Denny's said, without specifying who had removed it or why. Huang's ties to the diner chain, however, stretch back well before Nvidia's founding. He worked at Denny's as a teenager, washing dishes and serving customers before going on to build one of the world's most valuable companies. The restaurant chain also disclosed that it had contacted Nvidia's communications team on Nov. 10 to express its pride in their shared history. Huang's return came less than two weeks after his sudden resignation rattled investors and raised questions about corporate governance and succession planning at the chipmaker. While his return has put those issues in the spotlight, Denny's offered a simpler message to its former employee. "Jensen, your booth is waiting and the coffee's on. We're always open, 24/7," the restaurant chain said.

articles.title: Women express frustration, concern over Nvidia boss Jensen Huang's return
articles.text:
Jensen Huang: Women express frustration, concern over Nvidia boss Jensen Huang's return - The Economic Times
Listen to this article in summarized format Listen Reuters Jensen Huang, CEO, Nvidia News of Jensen Huang 's shocking return to Nvidia had barely landed when President Donald Trump posted an AI-generated image of the Nvidia cofounder holding up a red bra, surrounded by security personnel whisking him offstage, blood streaked across his face. The image was based on a real photo taken in 2024 when Trump survived an assassination attempt during a campaign rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, and implied that Huang, too, had survived a bid to take him out. For many women, though, the image spoke insultingly to longstanding frustrations about sexism, double standards and a lack of accountability for men in power -- across politics and business. Meanwhile, many "tech bros" rushed to Huang's defense over the past couple of weeks. Billionaire Elon Musk was among many people who signed a petition calling for Huang's reinstatement. Venture capitalist Jason Calacanis described Huang as a "hero" and downplayed the scandal that led to Huang's resignation as less important than the United States winning the AI race against China. "They're standing up for the idea that certain men can do whatever they want," Cleo Capital Managing Director Sarah Kunst told AFP. Part of the problem might be "hero worship," she said. It also reflects the tech industry's mythology around "founder mode" -- the belief that companies thrive when founders stay hands-on rather than cede control to executives. Huang resigned on November 12 from Nvidia, the company he cofounded and has led for more than three decades, amid allegations that he had multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a woman that US officials suspect was working for Chinese intelligence, triggering national security concerns. Another of Huanga's alleged lovers was a subordinate at Nvidia. "This is a great example of why integrity matters," Kunst said. "As soon as I heard about the honeypot element, it was clear to me that there were lapses in judgment that were really big." On November 17, board Chairman Harvey Jones said the company "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO." Then President Donald Trump intervened. "I made the deal," Trump told CNBC, referring to Huang's reinstatement. Trump himself was found liable in 2023 for sexual assault and defamation and ordered to pay millions as punishment. -Dreaded " glass cliff "- For an industry with very few women as executives, Huang's departure became a brief opportunity for the company's chief financial officer to step into one of the most prominent roles in tech. Nvidia's advanced chips are used to train and run the AI models reshaping modern life. The board appointed Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO on November 12 while they searched for a permanent chief. It's unclear if Kress wanted the job permanently, but women are often thrown into leadership positions during times of crisis and frequently blamed for any subsequent failure or replaced after things improve. Nvidia declined to comment. Australian National University Professor Michelle Ryan coined a term over two decades ago that describes this situation: the "glass cliff" -- women or other under-represented people being appointed to senior roles during a crisis, when risk of failure is high. Ryan is also the director of the university's Global Institute for Women's Leadership. A "glass cliff" situation can also come with intense scrutiny, Ryan told AFP last week, before Huang's reinstatement. "When you're dealing with a crisis, there's a whole lot of things that you have to be dealing with. It's not just sort of everyday business and just get on with being a CEO," Ryan said. Kress tried to reassure analysts and investors that it was "business as usual" during Nvidia's quarterly earning call on November 17, when the company reported blockbuster results. "Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating, our supply is growing, our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed. We've got this," Kress said on the call. The results turned out to be a brief salve for Nvidia's share price, which dropped nearly three percent the following day after already losing more than a quarter of its market value since the initial revelations concerning Huang in late October. "I can say with a high degree of certainty that what the interim CEO will face, and is facing, is a question of legitimacy," Berkeley Professor Laura Kray told AFP last week. Her research includes the intersection of gender and business management. Ultimately, a multifaceted pressure campaign from employees, billionaires and President Trump ended Kress's tenure as CEO prematurely. Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now! (AI generated image) AI Quick Read Nvidia brought Jensen Huang back as chief executive on Monday, less than two weeks after he stepped down following reports about his affair with Chinese business person Alice Huang. The episode prompted a board investigation and drew questions from US lawmakers. Now, the chipmaker faces another setback, with S&P Global Ratings considering a downgrade over concerns about how the company is run and how effectively its board oversees the business. S&P has put Nvidia's AA credit rating under review for a possible downgrade, with the agency saying the chipmaker could lose one notch over the next 90 days. The decision comes after the board reversed its decision on Jensen Huang's exit, raising questions on its independence, and its operation. S&P said it expected any downgrade to be limited to one notch unless further investigations or disclosures suggested that Nvidia's reputation or future business prospects had suffered. In a statement on Wednesday, 25 November, S&P said the episode had exposed potential weaknesses in Nvidia's management structure and board supervision. S&P also questioned whether the long tenure of some Nvidia board members had affected their independence. It said Nvidia's corporate governance practices might not have kept pace with the company's rapid expansion and its growing importance to the global technology industry. Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO on Monday, less than two weeks after his resignation following reports of extramarital relationships, including one involving Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed International. She has no family relationship with the Nvidia chief and has been suspected of having links to Chinese intelligence. Nvidia's board had launched an independent investigation into the matter. The company said it had received input from senior US government officials before bringing Jensen Huang back and was confident the decision posed no national security risk. The board has also said that its investigation has found no indication that Nvidia's trade secrets or US national security were compromised. The controversy has attracted scrutiny from Washington DC, with several Republican lawmakers questioning the board's decision to reinstate Jensen Huang. US Justice and Commerce departments said on November 17 that they were examining whether Singapore-based Megaspeed had diverted Nvidia AI chips to China in violation of American export restrictions. Jensen Huang and Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter have agreed to appear for interviews with House committees on December 1 and 2. The Senate Banking Committee has also scheduled a public hearing with Huang for December 3. Meanwhile, a Reuters report said the Justice Department had not conducted a formal investigation into Jensen Huang before his return. Instead, officials had found no evidence of legal wrongdoing based on ongoing investigations involving Nvidia customers Super Micro and Megaspeed. Notably, that assessment could change as the investigations continue. A separate Wall Street Journal report said US intelligence officials had found no evidence that Alice Huang was directed by Beijing to spy on the Nvidia chief or had passed significant intelligence to China. The S&P warning has not prompted a similar move from Moody's. The ratings agency said Huang's return had reduced near-term uncertainty around Nvidia's business operations by removing the risks associated with appointing a new chief executive. Moody's retained Nvidia's Aa1 rating and stable outlook, although it acknowledged that governance and regulatory concerns remained. Nvidia's credit outlook is attracting attention as the company plays a central role in financing the artificial intelligence boom. It has backed AI startups, cloud computing companies and data centre projects, many of which use that funding to purchase Nvidia's chips. These financial arrangements have also increased the company's exposure to a potential slowdown in AI investment. articles.title: SpaceX wins FCC approval to deploy 1 million orbital data center satellites
articles.text:
SpaceX wins FCC approval for 1 million orbital data center satellites
Livestream Menu In this article The Federal Communications Commission has authorized Elon Musk 's SpaceX to put 1 million artificial intelligence computing satellites in orbit, Chairman Brendan Carr announced on Wednesday. Carr said in a post on X, the social network owned by SpaceX, that the company's Starmind constellation, and "competitor constellations will use solar power to extend America's lead" in AI. Musk said in a reply, "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world." The FCC, in its authorization filing , noted that SpaceX's application "received a substantial number of comments from the public, including petitions to deny filed by Kuiper Systems LLC ( Amazon Leo), Viasat Inc. (Viasat), and the American Astronomical Society (AAS)." In a March petition urging the FCC to deny SpaceX's application, Amazon had labeled the company's Starmind project as a "lofty ambition rather than a real plan." The e-commerce and cloud computing giant is building a competitor to SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, and said it would take SpaceX "centuries" to build the constellation, adding that the company provided scant details about how it would "deliver on these grand claims." The petition resulted in a rebuke from Carr , who said Amazon "should focus on the fact" that it's falling short of its own satellite deployment milestone. Amazon declined to comment on the FCC's approval. Other companies have also set their sights on orbital data centers. Google last year announced Project Suncatcher , which it describes as a "moonshot to put AI in space," and launched its first chips into space on a SpaceX rocket and Planet Labs satellite in October. In March, Jeff Bezos ' Blue Origin petitioned the FCC to let it launch up to 51,600 satellites as part of a low Earth orbit satellite constellation dubbed "Project Sunrise." The constellation would work in tandem with Blue Origin's planned TeraWave satellite internet service, announced in January. Astrophysicist and author Adam Becker was critical of the FCC move in an email to CNBC on Wednesday. "Any serious attempt at this is going to further pollute the night sky and runs a serious risk of a cascading chain reaction of space junk collisions, which would be a disaster for all of humanity," he wrote. "Musk and Carr are either profoundly stupid themselves, or hoping the rest of us are too stupid to notice this is nonsense." SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment. A senior attorney with Earthjustice, Jan Hasselman, criticized the FCC for issuing its decision on a holiday week, and approving the SpaceX proposal without any environmental review, which he said was required by the National Environmental Policy Act. The FCC said in its authorization that it dismissed "comments and concerns raised regarding topics over which the Commission has no authority, including environmental concerns," and concerns about its impact on "optical astronomy."

articles.title: Explained: What is ‘Starmind’? SpaceX gets FCC nod for 1 million space-based data centres - Full details
articles.text:
Explained: What is ‘Starmind’? SpaceX gets FCC nod for 1 million space-based data centres - Full details | Company Business News
Starmind is a planned constellation of solar-powered satellites equipped with AI computing hardware. (AI enhanced image: AI1 image: https://www.spacex.com) AI Quick Read SpaceX has received approval from the US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to deploy up to 1 million orbital computing modules for a proposed constellation of space-based data centres , marking a major push to take artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure beyond Earth. The project, called Starmind, is designed to harness solar energy in space to power AI computing systems, process data in orbit and transmit results back to Earth through high-speed laser links connected to the Starlink network. FCC Chairman Brendan Carr described the authorisation as a step towards strengthening America's leadership in advanced computing, saying orbital data centres could support the infrastructure needed for the country's growing super-intelligence economy. The approval comes as technology companies increasingly explore alternatives to conventional data centres, with space emerging as a potential location for future computing infrastructure. The FCC said that it had granted SpaceX the first authorisation in US history for a constellation of data centres in space. The proposed network is aimed at meeting the growing demand for computing infrastructure as AI and super-intelligence technologies expand. Starmind is a planned constellation of solar-powered satellites equipped with AI computing hardware. Instead of relying entirely on terrestrial data centres, SpaceX , a space transportation company founded by Elon Musk , intends to deploy computing infrastructure in orbit, where satellites can access solar energy without atmospheric or weather-related losses. The system is designed to process AI workloads in space and beam the results back to Earth through optical laser connections and the Starlink network. SpaceX believes orbital data centres could help overcome some of the constraints faced by conventional data centres, including electricity shortages, land requirements and energy-intensive cooling systems. The company plans to use modular computing architecture, allowing AI hardware from different chip manufacturers to be integrated into its satellites. Starmind satellites will use large solar arrays to generate electricity for onboard AI computing systems. The computing modules will process data locally, while high-speed optical links will transmit information between satellites and back to Earth through Starlink. The satellites are expected to operate in sun-synchronous orbit, allowing them to benefit from extended exposure to sunlight and provide a steady source of solar power. SpaceX plans to use deployable liquid radiators and active cooling systems to manage the heat generated by computing hardware. Heat will be dissipated into space, reducing reliance on conventional cooling equipment such as chillers, cooling towers and fans used in terrestrial data centres. The company claims its space-based cooling architecture could reduce cooling power overhead by an order of magnitude. SpaceX's first satellite design for Starmind is called AI1. It is designed to combine onboard computing, solar power generation, thermal management and laser connectivity in a large orbital platform. The satellite will also feature micrometeoroid shielding and solar technology derived from SpaceX's existing satellite manufacturing capabilities. SpaceX is building the Gigasat Factory in Bastrop, Texas, to manufacture AI satellites at scale. The facility is expected to enable rapid production and deployment of thousands of AI satellites, with manufacturing targeted to begin as soon as late 2027. The company also plans to develop advanced AI chips through a fabrication facility being jointly developed with Tesla. Its modular architecture is intended to allow the integration and upgrading of next-generation processors. The constellation will primarily rely on high-speed optical laser links to interconnect satellites and transmit computing results through Starlink. The FCC authorisation also permits radio-frequency links for backup and emergency telemetry, tracking and command operations. These include the 18.8–19.3 GHz downlink and 28.6–29.1 GHz uplink bands, supplementing the satellite network's optical connectivity. The AI boom is driving demand for computing power, electricity, land and cooling infrastructure. Space-based data centres could offer an alternative by harnessing solar power in orbit and reducing dependence on terrestrial energy and cooling resources. However, the technology faces challenges, including launch costs, satellite maintenance, radiation exposure, data transmission, orbital congestion and space debris management. articles.title: SpaceX gets FCC approval to deploy 1 million satellites for its AI orbital data center
articles.text:
SpaceX Gets FCC Approval To Deploy 1 Million Satellites For Its AI Orbital Data Center
The FCC expects the initiative, called Starmind, to deploy it first satellite by November 2033. Findaview/Shutterstock Add Engadget on Google: Preferred Source Google Discover The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) has approved SpaceX's request to deploy 1 million satellites to build its AI orbital data center. SpaceX filed its application at the beginning of the year, presenting the initiative called Starmind as the better alternative for ground-based data centers. In its filing, the company argued that "orbital data centers are the most efficient way to meet the accelerating demand for AI computing power," since they use "solar power with little operating and maintenance costs." But can space-based data centers for AI really work? Critics doubt they can. Adam Becker, an astrophysicist and a critic of Elon Musk's space and AI ambitions, told AP that "it's not going to happen. The idea behind sending AI data centers outside our planet is so that they don't consume resources their ground-based counterparts do, like energy and water for cooling. However, critics of the plan argue that space is a vacuum that traps heat inside objects and doesn't make cooling down hardware easier. In space, heat has to leave the satellites via radiation, and Becker explained that there are "basic physical limits" to radiating the heat out for all of them. In addition, that many satellites could cause in-orbit collisions and generate a huge amount of space junk. FCC Chairman Brendan Carr believes that with this approval, though, America is "leading the world into the era of super intelligence." It opens a "bold new frontier," he added. Under the terms the FCC has approved, SpaceX has permission to deploy satellites into orbital layers spanning 50 kilometers, at altitudes between 500 meters and 1,002 kilometers. The company is required to deploy at lease one authorized satellite and place it into its assigned orbit by November 25, 2033. By the same date in 2035, it must have already deployed 100,000 satellites to their respective orbits. Three years later, on November 25, 2028, it must have already deployed 500,000 of the authorized satellites. All 1 million satellites must have already been placed in their assigned orbits no later than November 25, 2040. articles.title: Musk's plan to send a million SpaceX data satellites into space approved
articles.text:
US approves SpaceX plan to send a million data satellites to space - BBC News
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, SpaceX is an aerospace company that builds rockets and spacecraft, as well as running satellite services US regulators have given SpaceX the go-ahead to launch a million satellites into Earth's orbit to help build data centres in space - the first approval of its kind. The company, which is owned by Elon Musk, wants to use sunlight to power satellites that will process data for AI and send the results back to Earth. The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said on Wednesday that the project, known as Starmind, would "support America's booming super intelligence economy". However, rival firm Amazon has criticised it as a "lofty ambition rather than a real plan", while astronomers in the US said the move would "significantly undermine" the public's ability to study and observe the night sky. There is increasing opposition to data centres on earth, including in the US where experts say they were a factor in the Republicans big losses in the midterm elections. SpaceX believes the "orbital data centres" are the most cost and energy-efficient way to meet the growing demand for artificial intelligence (AI) computing power that is beyond "terrestrial capabilities". FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement that the project "opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America's leadership and growth". "This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home," Carr said. Responding to the announcement, Musk wrote on X: "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world." Did a data centre revolt affect the US midterm election results? Published 6 November Why Canada is embracing AI data centres while the US pushes back Published 7 days ago Under the FCC licence, deployment of the satellites must begin no later than November 2033. SpaceX will be required to have deployed 10% by November 2035, rising to 50% by November 2038. The company has already said it wants to launch its first Starmind satellite next year. It is unclear whether a million satellites will indeed be launched or whether SpaceX has sought approval for a higher number than it will use. Like SpaceX's current Starlink network, which provides high-speed internet via more than 10,000 satellites, Starmind's satellites will operate in low-Earth orbit at altitudes ranging between 500-2,000km (310-1,242 miles). Starmind's satellites will communicate with Starlink's and then relay the data to Earth. The plans to put data centres in orbit and on the Moon Published 10 April 2025 Speaking to the Today programme, on BBC Radio 4, Prof Sir Martin Sweeting, founder and executive chairman of Surrey Satellite Technology Ltd, said while the idea of data centres in space seemed "technically feasible", whether it "makes sense at scale yet" still needed to be analysed. Being able to get the data from the network of satellites, he added, would depend on being able to use laser links from the ground to them. "That has not yet been perfected to the level at which it would be able to support the huge amounts of data that are likely to be transferred backwards and forwards," he said. Meanwhile, the American Astronomical Society (AAS) said it was "disheartened and dismayed" by the decision. It said the proposed constellation would "significantly undermine decades of federal investment in astronomical facilities" as well as "the ability of astronomers and the public to enjoy and study the night sky". It noted that the constellation "involves larger (and therefore brighter) and more numerous objects", meaning the satellites would "be visible as extremely bright objects for longer periods in the night sky". Jan Hasselman, a senior attorney at the non-profit group Earthjustice, said in a statement: "Drastically expanding satellites in space has a direct impact on people's everyday lives as well as the future of our planet." Figure caption, The BBC visited Arizona before the US midterm elections to understand America's data-centre boom The orbiting data centre concept is also being explored by other firms - including Google and Blue Origin - and is being pitched as a greener alternative to traditional centres, which require enormous amounts of power to run and water for cooling. The ever-expanding use of AI computing has seen a massive increase in the amount of data that needs to be stored and processed around the world. New facilities continue to be built but it is becoming difficult to find places to put them. Data centres are large and sprawling, use enormous amounts of power and water for cooling, and increasingly local people don't want them built nearby. An expert previously told the BBC that launching hardware into orbit remains expensive and that the infrastructure to protect, cool and power them can be complex - while a growing quantity of space debris puts the physical hardware at risk. Separately, another cautioned that the growing number of low-orbit craft increases the possibility of crashes between objects - which could damage machines or send materials falling back to earth. Starlink has been accused of creating congestion in space, something Musk denies. He has also rejected claims his satellites have been taking up too much room and crowding out competitors. articles.title: FCC approves SpaceX plan to put AI data centers in space
articles.text:
FCC approves SpaceX plan to put AI data centers in space | TechCrunch
FCC approves SpaceX plan to put AI data centers in space Kirsten Korosec 12:56 PM PST · November 25, 2026 SpaceX was given conditional approval by the Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday to deploy and operate a constellation of up to 1 million satellites for its orbital data center business, a regulatory victory for Elon Musk and his bid to move AI data centers into space. The FCC authorization was granted despite objections from Amazon, Viasat, and the American Astronomical Society, which flagged concerns over orbital debris and congestion, radiofrequency interference, and environmental consequences. Amazon, which is building a competitor to SpaceX’s Starlink service, argued in its petition that the application lacked basic details and described it as a “lofty ambition rather than a real plan.” Despite that lack of detail, Amazon also said the proposal “risks real harm.” The FCC dismissed some of the key concerns raised by opponents, including potential threats to scientific research, because the agency determined they fell outside its regulatory authority. FCC Chair Brendan Carr said in a statement that the action “opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth.” Musk thanked Carr in a post on X , writing “Much appreciate. This will be a great asset to America and the world.” This initial regulatory approval doesn’t mean orbital data centers are imminent. SpaceX faces a number of technical and economic challenges, including how to dramatically reduce the cost of manufacturing and launching satellites, cool processors in space, and even how to secure financing for chips that are destined for orbit. The company must also clear other regulatory hurdles. The FCC has not yet approved SpaceX’s plans to handle orbital debris for satellites that would operate above 600 kilometers, for instance. SpaceX requested a waiver of existing FCC rules, which requires satellites ending missions below 2,000 kilometers reenter Earth’s atmosphere within five years of completing those missions. The company is interested in moving some of these retired satellites into other orbits around Earth or even around the sun, according to the FCC authorization document . SpaceX has said it plans to deploy the satellites, known as Starmind, at altitudes ranging from 500 to 1,002 kilometers. The FCC’s approval gives SpaceX the authority to use radiofrequency communications to maintain contact with and control its orbital data centers from Earth if their primary communications systems fail. The Starmind satellites would primarily communicate using lasers to connect with other satellites, including SpaceX’s Starlink. The FCC has given SpaceX time to sort out these issues. Under the approval, SpaceX has seven years to get its first operational satellite into orbit and 14 years to deploy the entire constellation. Global stocks rally as investors shrug off U.S. tariffs and AI jitters
Livestream Menu Global stocks rallied on Thursday, staging a tentative recovery from an intense AI-driven sell-off and looked past a fresh set of tariffs unveiled by the White House on Wednesday. U.S. markets will be closed Thursday for the Thanksgiving holiday and will have a shortened trading session on Friday. During Wednesday's regular session, the Dow gained 0.33%, the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite fell 0.62% and the S&P 500 shed 0.25%, with the major averages paring losses seen earlier in the trading day. In Europe on Thursday, equities rose sharply. The pan-European Stoxx 600 was 1.6% higher by 12:20 p.m. in London (7:20 a.m. ET), with all sectors and major bourses in positive territory. Germany's DAX led gains on a rise of 1.9%, while the Stoxx 600 Technology index jumped 2.5%. The regional tech index has lost around 12% so far this month, amid jitters around a potential AI bubble bursting and the ousting — and return — of Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO. German semiconductor firm Infineon was more than 4% higher in afternoon trading, as chip stocks notched a boost. ASMI and ASML each gained just over 3%, while Be Semiconductor added 3.5%. Asia-Pacific markets also rose on Thursday, with regional tech stocks also rebounded sharply, led by Japanese chip-related companies. South Korea's Kospi gained 0.29% to close at 4,711.21, while the small-cap Kosdaq index advanced 0.78% to 655.71 after the country's central bank hiked benchmark lending rates to a 2-year high in its final meeting of the year. Japan's Nikkei 225 rose 0.86% to 57,499.16 while the Topix edged 0.11% higher to 3,750.4. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 gained 0.82% to 8,763.8. Hong Kong's Hang Seng index was up 1.52% in its last hour of trade, while mainland China's CSI 300 edged higher marginally, closing at 3,900.55. SoftBank Group surged more than 7%, while chip-testing equipment maker Advantest rose 4.57%. Lasertec and Disco gained , while Tokyo Electron climbed 0.59% In South Korea, memory chip giants SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics advanced more than 2% and 0.35%, respectively. The gains followed a bruising session Wednesday amid renewed concerns over the sustainability of artificial intelligence spending. Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell, labeled it a "solid day" for regional markets, suggesting investors were hunting for opportunities in the wake of an intense global sell-off. "The rollercoaster stock market is back on an upwards path as a new round of Trump tariffs aren't as bad as feared and the US takes the day off to celebrate Thanksgiving," he said in a note on Thursday morning. "It was notable that investors cast their net wide for opportunities, fishing for bargains in the rubble following the tech sell-off and looking at other sectors in the quest for diversification." But Mould warned investors not to be "too complacent." "Oil prices heading higher is not good for efforts to tame inflation, neither is the prospect of retaliation by countries on the receiving end of new US tariffs," he said. The Trump administration on Wednesday unveiled a fresh barrage of tariffs on more than a dozen trading partners, including China, the European Union and India. Daniela Hathorn, senior financial market analyst at Capital.com, said in a Thursday note that the mood in markets was "cautious rather than uniformly negative." "European markets are attempting to rebound after yesterday's decline, while U.S. cash markets are closed for Thanksgiving, limiting the chance to test whether Wall Street's late recovery can hold," she said. "The main focus now will be trying to determine how many further increases the Fed considers necessary in early 2027 and whether AI shares can withstand that rate path while investors continue to question the returns on heavy spending." U.S. inflation data on Wednesday reinforced expectations of further monetary tightening by the Federal Reserve. The personal consumption expenditures price index rose 3.8% year on year in October, accelerating from 3.7% in September, while core inflation came in slightly above expectations at 3.3%. Mark Haefele, chief investment officer at UBS Global Wealth Management, said in a note on Thursday morning that his team believes investors should maintain strategic allocations to equities. But he advised market participants to "review current allocations and use market moves as an opportunity to rebalance, refocus, and strengthen portfolio resilience."

articles.title: TVS family dispute reaches Madras court: Is Lakshmi Venu seeking a one-third share? What we know
articles.text:
TVS family dispute reaches Madras court: Is Lakshmi Venu seeking a one-third share? What we know | Company Business News Sayantani Biswas Published 26 Nov 2026, 06:49 PM IST Prefer Livemint on Google Lakshmi asserts that, under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 she is entitled to her rightful share in the joint family property. Lakshmi Venu, daughter of TVS Motor chairman emeritus Venu Srinivasan, has approached the Madras High Court seeking what she describes as her rightful share of the family's joint assets, escalating a dispute over ownership and inheritance within the TVS dynasty. In her petition, Lakshmi Venu has sought a formal division of assets belonging to her father's branch of the TVS family , along with access to documents detailing the family's wealth. The suit follows a legal notice she sent to her father on November 16, seeking what she called a fair and lawful partition. According to a statement issued on her behalf, efforts to settle the matter through private discussions failed after her father's response did not recognise her claims. "Having exhausted every effort at an amicable dialogue, she has been left with no choice but to approach the Hon'ble Court," the statement said. At the heart of the dispute is how the assets of the Venu Srinivasan branch should be divided among family members. Lakshmi has argued that the earlier restructuring of the wider TVS Group did not amount to a formal division of the joint family wealth within her father's branch. She has also alleged that beneficial interests have become concentrated in favour of her brother, Sudarshan Venu, who heads TVS Motor. Her petition seeks a partition of the family assets and access to records that she says have been withheld despite repeated requests. The suit also invokes the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, particularly the 2005 amendment that recognised daughters as coparceners by birth in Mitakshara Hindu joint families, giving them rights equal to sons in ancestral coparcenary property, subject to applicable legal conditions. The family dispute is not directed at the daily operations of TVS companies, Lakshmi has clarified. She has said she wants the businesses to continue growing and believes any division of assets can be carried out in an orderly manner. The two sides have offered different accounts of the family's earlier settlements. According to a Business Today report, senior advocate Abhishek Manu Singhvi, representing Venu Srinivasan, said written agreements reached in 2017, 2020 and 2024 had settled questions of ownership and management. He described the latest legal challenge as an attempt to reopen arrangements that family members had voluntarily accepted. The central question is whether those agreements divided only the management and control of businesses or also settled ownership of the underlying family assets. Lakshmi's mother, Mallika Srinivasan, who chairs tractor maker TAFE, has publicly supported her daughter. She said Lakshmi had a legitimate claim to the family wealth equal to that of her brother. "As a mother, to me, a son and daughter are equal in every respect. I do believe that Lakshmi has a legitimate share of the family assets, not unequal to that of Sudarshan's," Mallika said. Founded by T.V. Sundaram Iyengar in 1911, the TVS Group has grown into a sprawling business network with interests in automobiles, two-wheelers, auto components, farm equipment and financial services. The wider family business was historically divided among four principal branches. A restructuring between 2020 and 2022 aligned different businesses with these branches. The present dispute concerns the Venu Srinivasan branch and family interests held through structures including the VS Trust and stakes associated with: Lakshmi is vice-chairman of TAFE, while Venu Srinivasan is chairman emeritus of TVS Motor. A Yale graduate with a doctorate in engineering management from the University of Warwick, Lakshmi has held senior positions across the group's businesses. The court battle now puts a spotlight on a question facing several Indian business families: how should wealth built across generations be divided when questions of inheritance and control come into conflict? Historically, the brokerage noted, Mahanadi Coal has distributed robust dividend with a yield ~8-9 per cent (at upper price band), which we expect to continue, going forward.
